analysis.one_liner: Ends professional baseball's exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill to make professional baseball subject to the antitrust laws never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from January 2023 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Professional baseball has enjoyed a unique exemption from the nation's antitrust laws — the rules against monopolies and unfair competition — since a 1922 Supreme Court ruling. This bill would have removed that carve-out, subjecting Major League Baseball and its teams to the same competition rules as other professional sports and businesses. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and received no further action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Baseball fans, minor-league players and cities, and rival leagues if they emerge. Baseball operates as the only major sport with a court-made exemption from antitrust law, which has protected league control over team locations, broadcast rights, ticketing, and the minor-league system. Applying antitrust law would let challenges to those arrangements proceed, opening the door to more competition, potential new teams, lower ticket and broadcast prices, and stronger bargaining power for players and minor-league clubs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fans, players, and prospective rival leagues

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that 'the antitrust laws shall apply to the business of providing for profit public baseball games between teams of professional baseball players and to leagues composed of such teams,' removing baseball's unique judicial carve-out. [S3]

The bill defines antitrust laws to include both the Clayton Act — the core law against unlawful restraints and monopolies — and the Federal Trade Commission Act's ban on unfair methods of competition, putting baseball under the same rules that apply across the economy. [S3] [S2]
The bill makes clear it applies only to conduct after enactment, so teams would not face liability for past arrangements. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Major League Baseball's team owners and the league office. The antitrust exemption is valuable property: it insulates the league's control over franchise placement, broadcast territories, and its monopoly over affiliated minor-league baseball. Owners would bear the cost of antitrust litigation risk and lose legal protection for practices such as restricting where teams can play or contractually boxing out rival leagues.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major League Baseball owners and league executives

drawbacks.text: Removing the exemption would expose baseball to litigation over decades-old league structures. Owners and some economists argue the exemption, whatever its origins, supports the league's stability — the controlled system of franchises and minor-league affiliates that keeps a schedule intact in every market. Challenges to relocation, broadcast territories, or the minor-league system could create years of legal uncertainty. [S3]

Antitrust scrutiny is not guaranteed to lower prices for fans. Winning an antitrust case requires proving harm, and courts could uphold existing league practices as reasonable, meaning fans could bear new litigation costs passed through ticket and broadcast prices without guaranteed benefit. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, well-defined fix: it puts baseball under the same competition rules every other major business already follows, while prospectively shielding past conduct. The main cost is litigation uncertainty for a league whose structures were built under a century of exemption. For fans, players, and cities, the upside is the possibility of challenging monopoly practices the exemption currently places beyond reach; the honest caveat is that courts, not this bill, would ultimately decide which practices fall.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025. [S5] [S1]

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Duncan of South Carolina introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, with two Republican cosponsors, Reps. Andy Biggs of Arizona and Dan Bishop of North Carolina. [S3] [S4]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is where the record ends. [S5]
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major League Baseball's owners and the league office are better off: they keep the antitrust exemption that shields their control over franchises, broadcasts, and the minor leagues, and no challenge to those arrangements can proceed under federal antitrust law.

for.name: Reps. Andy Biggs and Dan Bishop
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsors it attracted. [S4]

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 9, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship came from Republicans (the sponsor plus two Republican cosponsors out of 224 House Republicans), and no member publicly opposed it, so the partisan shape of the never-held vote is unknown. [S4] [S3]

industries.industry: Major League Baseball and its team owners
industries.note: The bill would strip baseball's unique antitrust exemption, exposing team and league control over franchise placement, broadcast territories, and the affiliated minor leagues to competition challenges for the first time since 1922. Fans pay the prices and face the market limits that exemption protects. [S3] [S2]

Minor-league clubs operate inside MLB's antitrust-shielded system, which has backed league control over affiliations and player conditions; ending the exemption would give minor-league teams and players new legal avenues, though it also injects uncertainty into the affiliation system they depend on. [S2]
